title: Quality guardrails + traffic experiments — Northbridge Analytics
summary: Redwood demo of Console Evaluate/Optimize: building prompt sets, creating regression alerts, setting up canary / traffic-split experiments, and integrating alerts into Slack and SRE workflows. Customer cares about failure modes, signal quality, annotation effort, and data residency. Next step: scoped pilot with 10k evals, run a canary traffic split for 2 weeks, and share security docs.
transcript:
[00:00] Alicia Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alicia from Redwood. We've got Tom and Nina on the line from engineering. How's everybody doing?
[00:06] Maya Singh: Good, thanks. Excited — we've been looking forward to this.
[00:08] Carlos Ruiz: Yep. Quick note, we're on a little delayed network but should be fine.
[00:12] Alicia Park: Great. Today we'll walk through how Redwood helps you detect prompt regressions and run traffic experiments so you can safely roll out new prompt variants or model updates. Tom, you want to kick off the console demo?
[00:22] Tom Breuer: Yeah, thanks. I'll share my screen — let me know if that doesn't come through.
[00:28] [screen share starts, brief pause] 
[00:31] Tom Breuer: Alright, so this is the Road — Redwood Console, Evaluate tab. First thing we do is create a prompt set, which is basically a curated collection of examples you care about, the golden outputs, and the metrics to watch. You can import a CSV or hook to S3.
[00:46] Leah Porter: What's the annotation workflow like? We have contractors who label.
[00:49] Nina Cho: Good question. We have an annotation UI — you can send tasks to internal reviewers or to AMT-like external annotators. You can also mark examples as "gold" for gating.
[00:58] Carlos Ruiz: Is there a limit on size of prompt sets? We typically work with 50k examples for model validation.
[01:03] Tom Breuer: You can scale to 100k-plus, but for realtime dashboards we sample; the bulk runs can be scheduled. The sampling is configurable by label, traffic weight, or recency.
[01:14] Maya Singh: Okay. We need to detect semantic drift, not just exact text diffs. What metrics do you compute?
[01:19] Tom Breuer: We support multiple metrics: string-based (exact match, token overlap), semantic similarity via embed cosine, and pairwise human preference aggregation. There's also custom thresholds and composite scores.
[01:30] Alicia Park: Important to call out: semantic similarity uses the embedding model you pick — you can use hosted Redwood embeddings or bring your own.
[01:36] Carlos Ruiz: Cool. Can you show a regression alert? How noisy are these?
[01:40] Tom Breuer: Sure. I'll open an alert rule — here's one that triggers when average pairwise preference drops by more than 6% over a 24-hour window. You can tune the baseline window and control for seasonality.
[01:51] [00:52] Tom Breuer: The rule evaluates against the golden set and a sliding baseline. If it trips, it creates a ticket and posts to Slack, plus optionally opens a fallback to the previous model or variant.
[01:59] Evan Holt: Fallbacks — can that be automatic? We want immediate rollback for significant regressions.
[02:04] Nina Cho: Yes, you can set automatic rollback policies with safe thresholds, or just alert the SRE and block rollout until manual sign-off.
[02:11] Maya Singh: How do you prevent false positives? We had a vendor that spammed alerts every release.
[02:16] Tom Breuer: Two levers: first, set the alert to aggregate over meaningful slices — per-customer, per-route, per-intent; second, require a minimum sample size and use bootstrapped confidence intervals, reduces sensitivity to outliers. Also you can exclude noisy traffic with labels.
[02:32] Carlos Ruiz: You mentioned traffic splits — show how we run a canary?
[02:36] Tom Breuer: Sure. Under Deploy -> Experiments, we create an experiment that splits traffic 90/10 between baseline and candidate. We attach the same prompt set and metrics to it. The experiment dashboard shows lift/loss, p-values, and an automated runbook suggestion.
[02:50] [03:00] Tom Breuer: Example: here's a canary we ran internally — 7 days, monitored pairwise win rate and latency. The console surfaced a 3.2% drop with p=0.03, and flagged it as fail. We then rolled back automatically.
[03:12] Maya Singh: How do you compute p-values on non-iid data? Our traffic has heavy seasonality.
[03:18] Tom Breuer: We use block bootstrap and stratified sampling by time window and user-agent slices. You can also run a permutation test if you need stricter nonparametric inference.
[03:28] Leah Porter: Integration question — we send alerts to PagerDuty and have a complicated incident playbook.
[03:32] Alicia Park: We have built-in integrations: Slack, PagerDuty, webhook, Jira. The webhook payload includes sample IDs, metric deltas, and links to the annotation viewer for quick triage.
[03:43] Carlos Ruiz: Does the webhook contain raw prompts? We have PII concerns.
[03:46] Nina Cho: You can redact fields on export, or hash prompt IDs. There's also an option to keep all PII in your VPC if you're on Private deployment.
[03:55] Maya Singh: Security docs? We need SOC 2, KMS details, HSM integration.
[03:59] Alicia Park: We'll share the security pack after the call. We support SOC 2 Type II, bring-your-own-KMS, and on-prem control plane for air-gapped setups.
[04:08] Evan Holt: Great. For metrics, can we do weighted metrics — like business value weighted by account ARR?
[04:14] Tom Breuer: Yes, we support custom aggregations — you can assign metadata to examples (account_id, ARR bucket) and compute weighted means.
[04:20] [04:22] Maya Singh: Show us the A/B comparison UI for human-review pairwise.
[04:25] Tom Breuer: Sure, here's the pairwise reviewer interface. Annotators see two candidate outputs side-by-side with the golden reference and pick preference or label tie. The UI shows inter-annotator agreement and flags low-confidence items for adjudication.
[04:39] Leah Porter: Do you provide a training set for our annotators, like guidelines?
[04:42] Nina Cho: We provide templates and best-practice rubrics; we can also run an initial calibration batch and compute rater reliability (Krippendorff's alpha) so you know annotation quality.
[04:53] Carlos Ruiz: How do we link evaluation to the API traffic? Our routes vary by feature flags.
[04:57] Tom Breuer: Each request can carry a route tag. You can configure prompt sets to map to specific routes or feature flags. In experiments you can slice by route and run per-route rollouts.
[05:08] Maya Singh: Latency — when we run pairwise annotation at scale, does Redwood do evals synchronously or asynchronously?
[05:13] Tom Breuer: Evals are asynchronous. For each request we store the sample and run batches through the eval workers; you can get near-real-time if you enable streaming of samples to the evaluator. But for heavy scale we recommend scheduled bulk scoring.
[05:25] Evan Holt: Quick architecture question: are the eval workers in our VPC or on Redwood infra?
[05:30] Nina Cho: Depends on deployment. Hosted uses Redwood-managed workers. For Dedicated we can run workers in dedicated capacity, and for Private your eval workers run in your VPC or on-prem per the package.
[05:40] [05:42] Maya Singh: Example edge case: a small but critical customer sees a 10% drop on our finance answers. How do we get per-customer alerts?
[05:50] Tom Breuer: We show per-customer slices and support alert rules targeted at a specific account_id or customer tag. If the sample size is small we use Bayesian shrinkage to avoid over-reacting while still surfacing signal.
[06:02] Carlos Ruiz: We need reporting for compliance — audit logs and who approved rollouts.
[06:06] Alicia Park: Console audit trails include who created experiments, approvals, timestamps, and the diff of configuration, exportable as CSV for audits.
[06:15] Maya Singh: Can you demo an incident flow — alert to triage to rollback?
[06:19] Tom Breuer: Yep. I'll simulate a regression trigger.
[06:22] [06:25] Tom Breuer: Alert fires, Slack message posts to #model-alerts with a link. Clicking the link opens the annotation viewer where you can see failing examples, the metric delta, and suggested remediation (tweak prompt, revert model, or increase sample size). There's a one-click rollback button that triggers the router to shift traffic back.
[06:41] Evan Holt: Nice. How do you validate that rollback actually mitigates user impact?
[06:45] Tom Breuer: The experiment timeline re-evaluates post-rollback; if metrics recover we mark the rollback successful and attach the evidence to the incident ticket.
[06:53] Leah Porter: On cost — do these evals add significant token costs?
[06:57] Nina Cho: There is cost; Optimize suggests sampling strategies and caching to limit eval token usage. For example, prefix caching avoids re-encoding shared context. We also recommend running some checks with smaller context windows or quantized candidate models for cheap signal.
[07:12] Carlos Ruiz: What about embedding costs — we rely heavily on a particular embed model for cosine similarity.
[07:16] Tom Breuer: You can cache embeddings and set TTLs. Also we support bringing your own embeddings if you run them in your infra.
[07:23] Maya Singh: For the pilot, we want a 2-week canary on two high-risk routes plus an audit report. What's a reasonable sample size?
[07:30] Tom Breuer: For detecting a 5% lift/loss with 80% power you'd typically want ~3k examples per arm, but stratification increases required numbers. We can help with a pre-run power analysis.
[07:41] Alicia Park: We'll include a recommended sampling plan in the pilot proposal.
[07:44] [07:46] Evan Holt: Can we set up role-based access so product folks can see dashboards but can't change rollout policies?
[07:51] Nina Cho: Yes, fine-grained RBAC. We also support SSO/SAML and SCIM for provisioning.
[07:58] Carlos Ruiz: Any gotchas with private deployments? Our security team pushes back on remote telemetry.
[08:02] Alicia Park: For Private, telemetry can be routed to your ELK/Datadog; we support local-only logs and optional anonymization.
[08:09] Maya Singh: Okay, I'd like to see the plan with timelines and costs.
[08:13] Alicia Park: We'll follow up with a pilot SOW. Quick recap and next steps at the end.
[08:18] Tom Breuer: A couple more product notes: the experiment engine supports multi-armed tests not just 2-way, and you can chain experiments over time for phased rollouts. Also Optimize will surface quantization recommendations to reduce candidate model compute during eval.
[08:31] Maya Singh: You said quantization recommendations — any impact on metric fidelity?
[08:34] Tom Breuer: There can be small differences; we recommend running a cross-check between quantized candidate and full-precision model on a smaller golden set to calibrate.
[08:44] Leah Porter: For our annotator team, how do we export tasks? We use internal tooling.
[08:48] Nina Cho: Exports to CSV, JSONL, or direct integration with Labelbox/Scale.
[08:53] Evan Holt: Will you send example payloads for webhooks?
[08:56] Alicia Park: Yes, we'll include webhook schema in the security pack.
[08:59] [09:00] Maya Singh: Alright, let's do a quick Q&A before we close. Carlos?
[09:03] Carlos Ruiz: Two quick ones: does Redwood keep copies of raw prompts for hosted customers? And how long are eval logs retained?
[09:10] Alicia Park: For hosted, by default we store eval logs 90 days; retention can be extended. If you require no storage, there are Private options. Raw prompts can be redacted in exports.
[09:20] Carlos Ruiz: Second — do you integrate with feature flagging tools like LaunchDarkly?
[09:24] Tom Breuer: Yes, we can integrate with LaunchDarkly and other flagging systems to drive traffic splits based on flags.
[09:30] Leah Porter: Last one — will you run a quick calibration batch with our annotators?
[09:33] Alicia Park: Absolutely. That's part of the pilot.
[09:36] [09:38] Alicia Park: Okay, quick recap of next steps and owners.
[09:41] Maya Singh: Thanks everyone.
[09:42] [END OF TRANSCRIPT]
